newsitem.title: LEBANON: GAMES-SECURITY FORCES QUELL NEAR-RIOT AS PAN ARAB GAMES OPEN.
newsitem.headline: GAMES-SECURITY FORCES QUELL NEAR-RIOT AS PAN ARAB GAMES OPEN.

text.p: The Pan Arab Games, the biggest international event Lebanon has staged since the 15-year civil war ended in 1990, opened on Saturday amid gunfire, a near-riot and an embarrassing diplomatic confrontation with Iraq.
The opening of the two-week long Games was tarnished by gunfire and a near-riot at the gates of the stadium when police stopped a large crowd from forcing their way in.

Witnesses said security forces called in fire trucks to hose down the crowd to stop them entering, but some of the crowd stoned the security forces, who fired in the air with automatic rifles to disperse them.
Despite the mayhem, there were no injuries, witnesses said.
Athletes from Somalia and Iraq were absent from the opening ceremony which included a pageant of 2,000 athletes from 19 Arab countries which was watched by 50,000 fans.
Organisers said Somalia never responded to invitations to compete, and Lebanese officials said Beirut banned Iraq from the games under pressure from Kuwait and Saudi Arabia, Iraq's Gulf War foes.
The ban caused an embarrassing two-day stand-off after Iraq sent its team to compete -- only to be turned back at the Lebanese border.
Almost 100 Iraqi athletes and officials arrived at a Lebanese border on Friday morning and waited nearly 36 hours for permission to enter before turning back for Baghdad.

Lebanon, which has no diplomatic relations with Iraq, made no official announcement that it was barring the Iraqi team, but officials in Beirut said Kuwait and Saudi Arabia had threatened to boycott the games if Iraq participated.
"Gulf money comes first in the politics of sport," said a headline in Beirut's English-language Daily Star newspaper commenting on Iraq's exclusion.
Saudi Arabia and Kuwait are among the biggest Arab contributors to Lebanon's post-war reconstruction and gave most of the money to rebuild the sports stadium.

Smarting at the humiliation, a Baghdad newspaper demanded on Saturday that Iraq lodge a complaint against the Lebanese organising committee at the World Court of Justice for refusing to let it compete.

The games, which are scheduled to take place every four years, were due to be held in 1996, but were delayed until now because the stadium, destroyed during the War and rebuilt at a cost of $50 million was not ready in time.

The government of billionaire Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri, which has made big strides in rebuilding the country, sees the event as proof that Lebanon has re-emerged from the chaos and destruction of the civil war to rejoin the international community.
Hariri and President Elias Hrawi made no mention of Iraq's exclusion in their inaugural speeches for the games but thanked Kuwait and Saudi Arabia for helping to rebuild the stadium.
